name: Prosecco
style: Italian sparkling wine: crisp, bubbly, green-apple fruity
why: Light, bubbly and fruity without being heavy. It's basically a celebration in a glass that goes with almost any snack.
funFact: On Prosecco labels, "Extra Dry" is actually sweeter than "Brut." Wine labels confuse everyone, so you're in good company.
lookFor: Any Prosecco DOC. "Brut" if you like it drier, "Extra Dry" if you like it a touch sweeter.

name: Champagne
style: French sparkling wine: toasty, crisp, fine bubbles
why: Crisp, toasty and full of tiny bubbles. It makes any meal feel like an occasion, even fried chicken or potato chips (a famously great match).
funFact: In most of the world, only sparkling wine from the Champagne region of France can be called Champagne. Similar bubbles from elsewhere in France are called Crémant, often at a fraction of the price.
lookFor: Any "Brut" Champagne. On a budget? Try a French Crémant instead.

name: Sauvignon Blanc
style: Zesty white wine: citrus, green herbs, mouthwatering
why: Zingy and fresh, like a squeeze of lime with a handful of herbs. It wakes up salads, seafood, goat cheese and anything green.
funFact: Sancerre (Sauvignon Blanc from France's Loire Valley) and Crottin de Chavignol goat cheese come from the same area. Sommeliers sum it up as "what grows together goes together."
lookFor: New Zealand bottles for big citrus flavor; Sancerre or Touraine from France for something subtler.

name: Off-Dry Riesling
style: Aromatic white wine: peach, lime, a touch of sweetness
why: Juicy and peachy with a hint of sweetness and lots of freshness. It's the classic answer to "what do I drink with spicy takeout?"
funFact: Thanks to its high acidity, Riesling is one of the few white wines that can age for decades.
lookFor: German "Kabinett" or "Spätlese," or any label that says "off-dry" or "medium sweet."

name: Pinot Grigio
style: Easygoing white wine: light, crisp, pear and lemon
why: Light, crisp and uncomplicated, the easy-drinking white. It won't overpower delicate food like fish, salads or light pasta.
funFact: Pinot Grigio and Pinot Gris are the same grape: Grigio is the Italian name, Gris the French. Both mean "gray," after the grape's grayish-pink skin.
lookFor: Italian Pinot Grigio from Alto Adige or Friuli tends to have more flavor than the cheapest bottles.

name: Oaked Chardonnay
style: Full, rich white wine: butter, vanilla, baked apple
why: Round, creamy and a little buttery. It has the body to match creamy pastas, roast chicken and anything with a rich sauce.
funFact: Chardonnay is the grape behind white Burgundy, and Champagne labeled "Blanc de Blancs" is made from 100% Chardonnay.
lookFor: California Chardonnay usually signals "buttery and oaky"; the back label often mentions oak or vanilla.

name: Dry Rosé
style: Pink wine: strawberry, watermelon, crisp and dry
why: Fresh strawberry and watermelon flavors with a crisp, dry finish. It's the ultimate "works with everything" wine for picnics and snack boards.
funFact: Most rosé is made from red grapes. The pink color comes from letting the juice touch the grape skins for just a few hours instead of weeks.
lookFor: Provence-style rosé (pale pink) for dry and crisp.

name: Pinot Noir
style: Light red wine: cherry, earthy, silky and smooth
why: A light, silky red with cherry and earthy notes. It's gentle enough for salmon but has enough flavor for mushrooms and roast chicken.
funFact: After the 2004 movie Sideways, where the main character raves about Pinot Noir (and trashes Merlot), US Pinot Noir sales jumped. Economists call it "the Sideways effect."
lookFor: Oregon, California's Central Coast, or "Bourgogne Rouge" from France.

name: Cabernet Sauvignon
style: Bold red wine: blackcurrant, oak, firm and dry
why: Big, bold and dry with dark-fruit flavor. It's the classic steakhouse red because it stands up to juicy, fatty meat.
funFact: In the 1990s, DNA testing at UC Davis showed Cabernet Sauvignon is a natural cross between Cabernet Franc and Sauvignon Blanc: a red and a white grape.
lookFor: California, Washington State or Chile for fruit-forward, approachable bottles.

name: Malbec
style: Juicy red wine: plum, blackberry, smooth and plush
why: Plummy and plush with softer edges than Cabernet. It's a crowd-pleasing red for burgers, BBQ and grilled anything.
funFact: Malbec originally comes from southwest France (around Cahors), but Argentina made it famous. Most Malbec you'll see today is from Mendoza.
lookFor: Argentine Malbec from Mendoza, which is great value under $15.

name: Chianti
style: Tuscan red wine: tart cherry, herbs, tangy
why: Tangy red with tart cherry and herbs. Its natural zip is exactly what tomato sauce needs, which is why it's the red-sauce Italian classic.
funFact: The old-school straw-wrapped Chianti bottle is called a "fiasco." In Italian that just means "flask."
lookFor: "Chianti" or "Chianti Classico" (look for the black rooster on the neck).

name: Moscato d'Asti
style: Sweet, lightly fizzy white wine: peach, honey, orange blossom
why: Sweet, peachy and gently fizzy, with low alcohol. Perfect with fruity desserts, and it cools down spicy food too.
funFact: Moscato d'Asti is usually only about 5 to 6% alcohol, roughly the same as a beer, which makes it an easy-going sipper.
lookFor: "Moscato d'Asti" from Italy, which is fresher and more delicate than generic Moscato.

name: Mexican Lager
style: Light, crisp beer, great with a lime wedge
why: Ice-cold, crisp and refreshing. It puts out the fire from spicy food and keeps you coming back for another chip.
funFact: Mexico's brewing tradition got a boost from German and Austrian immigrants in the 1800s, which is why some Mexican beers are amber "Vienna-style" lagers.
factCheck: VERIFY: Austrian/German brewing influence on Mexican lager (commonly linked to the Maximilian era, 1860s). Widely repeated but double-check the phrasing.
lookFor: Any Mexican-style lager; add a lime wedge.

name: IPA
style: Hoppy beer: citrusy, piney, pleasantly bitter
why: Hoppy, citrusy and a little bitter. That bitterness is a great reset button after rich, cheesy, greasy bites like burgers.
funFact: The name "India Pale Ale" comes from hoppy pale ales shipped from England to British India in the 1800s. Hops helped preserve the beer on the long voyage.
factCheck: VERIFY: The IPA origin story is popular but partly debated by beer historians. The version here is kept deliberately modest.
lookFor: West Coast IPAs are more bitter and piney; Hazy/New England IPAs are juicier and softer.

name: Hefeweizen (Wheat Beer)
style: Cloudy German wheat beer: banana, clove, soft and bubbly
why: Soft, bubbly and fruity with almost no bitterness. It's great with brunch, sausages, salads and lightly spicy food.
funFact: The banana and clove flavors in Hefeweizen don't come from fruit or spices. They're made naturally by the special yeast.
lookFor: German Hefeweizen or any American "wheat beer."

name: Stout
style: Dark beer: roasted coffee, chocolate, creamy
why: Roasty, chocolatey and creamy, like coffee and dessert in one glass. It loves chocolate cake, hearty stews and even oysters.
funFact: Guinness looks black, but hold it up to the light and it's actually a very dark ruby red. Stout and oysters is also a classic Irish pairing.
lookFor: Guinness or any "milk stout" (a sweeter, softer style).

name: Saison
style: Belgian farmhouse ale: dry, peppery, lively bubbles
why: Dry, peppery and super bubbly. It's one of the most food-friendly beers out there, from cheese boards to roast chicken.
funFact: Saisons (French for "seasons") were originally brewed on farms in the French-speaking part of Belgium as a refreshing drink for seasonal farm workers.
lookFor: Saison Dupont is the classic; many craft breweries make one too.

name: Hard Cider
style: Fermented apple drink: crisp, fruity, lightly sweet
why: Crisp apple, a little sweet and bubbly. Apples and pork are best friends, and cider brings that same magic to pork chops, sausages and cheese.
funFact: Johnny Appleseed's apple trees were mostly the tart kind used for cider, not for eating. In early America, cider was an everyday drink.
factCheck: VERIFY: The Johnny Appleseed/cider claim is popular (e.g. Michael Pollan's The Botany of Desire) but worth confirming before presenting as fact.
lookFor: "Dry" cider if you like it less sweet. Technically not a beer, but it lives in the beer aisle.

name: Bourbon
style: American whiskey: caramel, vanilla, warm and sweet-ish
why: Warm caramel and vanilla, sipped neat or on one big ice cube. It's a natural with smoky BBQ and pecan pie.
funFact: Bourbon must be aged in brand-new charred oak containers (that's where the caramel and vanilla come from). And it doesn't have to be made in Kentucky; any US state works.
lookFor: A "wheated" bourbon for a softer, smoother sip.

name: Tequila Blanco
style: Unaged agave spirit: peppery, citrusy, bright
why: Bright, peppery and fresh. Sip it slowly with lime alongside ceviche, grilled fish or anything with fresh salsa.
funFact: Real tequila must be made from blue Weber agave, mostly in the Mexican state of Jalisco. The agave plant takes years to mature before it's harvested.
lookFor: Labels that say "100% de agave."

name: Aged Rum
style: Golden rum: brown sugar, vanilla, warm spice
why: Smooth brown sugar and vanilla, like dessert you can sip. Lovely with grilled pineapple, caramel desserts or smoky meat.
funFact: Britain's Royal Navy gave sailors a daily ration of rum (a "tot") for over 300 years, until it ended on July 31, 1970, a day still known as "Black Tot Day."
lookFor: Rums from Barbados, Jamaica or Guatemala labeled "aged" or "añejo."

name: Smoky Scotch
style: Peated Scotch whisky: campfire smoke, sea salt, bold
why: Big campfire smoke with a salty edge. An adventurous pick, amazing with smoked meats, aged cheese or dark chocolate.
funFact: That smoky flavor comes from drying malted barley over peat fires. It's most famous on the Scottish island of Islay.
lookFor: Islay single malts. Add a few drops of water to soften it.

name: Irish Cream Liqueur
style: Cream liqueur: chocolate, vanilla, whiskey, silky
why: Silky, sweet and chocolatey, like a grown-up milkshake. Pour it over ice with dessert or into your coffee.
funFact: Baileys, the original Irish cream, was launched in 1974. Blending cream with whiskey so it stays fresh on the shelf was a big food-science challenge.
lookFor: Baileys or a store-brand Irish cream; serve over ice.

name: Classic Margarita
style: Tequila, lime, orange liqueur: tangy, bright, salty rim
why: Tangy lime, a little sweetness and a salty rim. It was practically built for tacos and chips-and-guac night.
funFact: At least half a dozen people claim to have invented the margarita, and nobody agrees on who really did. Everyone wants credit for a hit.
lookFor: Tequila blanco, triple sec and fresh limes (2 : 1 : 1). Salt the rim.

name: Mojito
style: Rum, lime, mint, soda: minty, fizzy, refreshing
why: Cool mint, fresh lime and bubbles. It's like air-conditioning for spicy or fried food.
funFact: The mojito comes from Cuba and is often linked to Ernest Hemingway, though historians doubt that the famous "My mojito in La Bodeguita" note was really written by him.
factCheck: VERIFY: The Hemingway/La Bodeguita attribution is widely considered apocryphal. The copy says so, but confirm before presenting.
lookFor: White rum, fresh mint, limes, sugar and club soda.

name: Vodka Martini (with Olives)
style: Vodka, dry vermouth, olives: crisp, cold, savory
why: Ice-cold, crisp and savory from the olive brine. It's a classy match for salty, rich bites like oysters, cheese or a fancy dinner.
funFact: James Bond made the vodka martini "shaken, not stirred" one of the most famous drink orders in pop culture. Bartenders usually stir martinis, which is exactly why Bond's order stood out.
lookFor: A good vodka, dry vermouth and green olives (add a splash of brine for a "dirty" martini).

name: Aperol Spritz
style: Aperol, Prosecco, soda: bittersweet orange, bubbly
why: Bubbly, bittersweet orange that's light on alcohol and big on sunshine. It's Italy's favorite pre-dinner drink with salty snacks.
funFact: Aperol was created in Padua, Italy in 1919. "Spritz" comes from the German word for "splash," reportedly from Austrian soldiers who added a splash of water to Veneto wines in the 1800s.
factCheck: VERIFY: The Aperol 1919/Padua date is well established; the Austrian-soldiers origin of "spritz" is a common story but less certain.
lookFor: Aperol, Prosecco, soda water and an orange slice (3 : 2 : 1).

name: Paloma
style: Tequila and grapefruit soda: tart, fizzy, refreshing
why: Tart grapefruit, a pinch of salt and lots of bubbles. It's lighter and easier than a margarita, and great with spicy tacos.
funFact: "Paloma" means "dove" in Spanish. It's a simple two-ingredient highball: tequila plus grapefruit soda.
lookFor: Tequila blanco and grapefruit soda (Jarritos or Squirt), plus a squeeze of lime.

name: Old Fashioned
style: Whiskey, sugar, bitters, orange: rich, warm, smooth
why: Warm whiskey rounded off with a little sugar and orange. It's cozy and classic, great with steak, burgers or a brownie.
funFact: It's one of the oldest cocktails around. An 1806 newspaper defined a "cock-tail" as spirits, sugar, water and bitters, which is basically an Old Fashioned.
lookFor: Bourbon or rye, a sugar cube, Angostura bitters and an orange peel.

name: Hot Toddy
style: Whiskey, honey, lemon, hot water: warm and soothing
why: Warm honey and lemon with a gentle whiskey glow, like a hug in a mug. Nice with soups, simple roasts or cookies.
funFact: Hot toddies have been a cold-weather staple in Scotland and Ireland for generations, and a classic folk remedy for sore throats (not a medical one!).
factCheck: VERIFY: Keep this generic. Specific origin stories for the word "toddy" (e.g. from a Hindi word for palm wine) are debated.
lookFor: Any whiskey, honey, a lemon and a cinnamon stick if you have one.

name: Espresso Martini
style: Vodka, espresso, coffee liqueur: rich, sweet, frothy
why: Coffee, a little sweetness and a frothy top. It's dessert and an after-dinner coffee in one, great with tiramisu or chocolate.
funFact: London bartender Dick Bradsell created it in the 1980s, reportedly for a customer who asked for a drink that would "wake me up."
factCheck: VERIFY: Dick Bradsell and the 1980s are well established; the exact customer quote varies between retellings, so it's kept vague.
lookFor: Vodka, cold espresso or cold brew concentrate and coffee liqueur. Shake hard for the foam.

name: Whisky Highball
style: Whisky and soda over ice: light, crisp, bubbly
why: Whisky stretched with lots of cold bubbles, so it's light, crisp and refreshing. It's amazing with fried chicken, yakitori and sushi.
funFact: Whisky highballs are a staple at Japanese izakayas (casual pubs), where they're famously paired with karaage fried chicken.
lookFor: Any smooth whisky (Japanese blends are classic), very cold club soda and lots of ice.

name: Merlot
style: Soft red wine: plum, black cherry, smooth and round
why: Plush, plummy and gentle, a red with soft edges and no harsh grip. Easy with burgers, roast chicken and mushroom dishes.
funFact: Merlot is one of the main grapes of Bordeaux, and Pétrus, one of the world's most famous and expensive wines, is made almost entirely from it.
lookFor: Merlot from California, Washington State or Chile for soft, fruity bottles.

name: Zinfandel
style: Jammy red wine: ripe berries, black pepper, bold
why: Big, jammy and a little peppery. Its ripe fruit is a natural match for sweet-and-smoky BBQ sauce, ribs and pizza.
funFact: DNA testing showed that Zinfandel is the same grape as Italy's Primitivo and Croatia's Crljenak Kaštelanski. (Sweet pink "White Zinfandel" is made from it too.)
lookFor: Red Zinfandel from California (Lodi and Sonoma are classic regions).

name: Syrah / Shiraz
style: Dark red wine: blackberry, black pepper, smoky
why: Dark, peppery and a little smoky. It stands up to lamb, grilled steak and sausages like it was made for them.
funFact: Syrah and Shiraz are the same grape. "Shiraz" is the name Australia made famous, and it usually signals a riper, jammier style.
lookFor: Australian Shiraz for juicy and bold; French Côtes du Rhône for a smoother, earthier red.

name: Red Blend
style: Crowd-pleasing red: ripe dark fruit, smooth, a touch sweet
why: Juicy, smooth and easy to like, the "something for everyone" red. Great with burgers, pizza and a cheese board.
funFact: Blending isn't cheating. Most red Bordeaux is a blend of grapes like Cabernet Sauvignon and Merlot, mixed to get the best of each.
lookFor: Any bottle labeled "Red Blend." California blends are fruit-forward and smooth.

name: Sparkling Rosé
style: Pink bubbly: strawberry, cream, lively bubbles
why: Strawberry-scented bubbles with a soft, slightly sweet finish. It turns brunch, seafood or fried chicken into a celebration.
funFact: Rosé Champagne is one of the few European wines where winemakers may make pink wine by blending a little red wine into white.
lookFor: Sparkling rosé from Spain (Cava Rosado), France (Crémant Rosé) or California.

name: Shandy
style: Beer + lemonade: light, citrusy, refreshing
why: Half beer, half lemonade: lighter, sweeter and super refreshing. Perfect for brunch, salads and a sunny afternoon.
funFact: In Germany it's called a Radler ("cyclist"). The popular story is that a Bavarian innkeeper created it in the 1920s to stretch his beer for a crowd of thirsty cyclists.
factCheck: VERIFY: The Radler/Franz Kugler cyclist story (1922) is widely repeated but may be legend.
lookFor: A pre-mixed lemon shandy or Radler, or mix a light lager with lemonade 50/50.

name: Vodka (Ice-Cold)
style: Clean, neutral spirit: crisp, smooth, served very cold
why: Clean and ice-cold, sipped in small amounts. It's the classic partner for salty, rich bites like smoked salmon, caviar and pickles.
funFact: The word "vodka" comes from the Slavic word for water ("voda"), so it roughly means "little water."
lookFor: A mid-priced vodka kept in the freezer; serve in small, chilled glasses.

name: Gin
style: Botanical spirit: juniper, citrus peel, herbs
why: Piney, herbal and citrusy. A gin & tonic with seafood, oysters or charcuterie is fresh, zingy and easy.
funFact: Gin gets its signature piney flavor from juniper berries, and its name comes from "genever," the Dutch juniper spirit it descends from.
lookFor: A London Dry gin plus tonic water and a lime or cucumber slice.

name: Irish Whiskey
style: Smooth whiskey: honey, vanilla, light and mellow
why: Smooth, honeyed and gentle, one of the easiest whiskeys to sip. Cozy with stew, chocolate or bread pudding.
funFact: Irish whiskey is traditionally distilled three times, one reason it's known for being so smooth. And it's spelled with an "e," unlike Scotch whisky.
lookFor: Any Irish whiskey; sip neat, on ice, or with a splash of water.

name: Cognac / Brandy
style: Aged grape brandy: dried fruit, caramel, warm spice
why: Warm and velvety with dried fruit and caramel. A slow, after-dinner sip with aged cheese, dark chocolate or a special steak dinner.
funFact: Cognac is brandy that must come from the Cognac region of France. The letters on the label (VS, VSOP, XO) tell you how long it was aged.
lookFor: VS or VSOP Cognac; any French or American brandy is a budget-friendly swap.

name: Spiced Rum
style: Rum with vanilla and baking spice: sweet, warm
why: Vanilla, cinnamon and brown sugar. Mixed with cola or ginger beer, it's great with jerk chicken, BBQ and pineapple desserts.
funFact: Most rum is made from molasses, the dark, sticky by-product of turning sugarcane into sugar. Spiced rum adds flavors like vanilla and cinnamon.
lookFor: Any spiced rum; mix with cola or ginger beer and a lime wedge.

name: Mimosa
style: Sparkling wine + orange juice: bright, bubbly, brunchy
why: Sunny orange juice plus bubbles, light and easy. Brunch's best friend with eggs, pastries and fruit.
funFact: It's named after the yellow mimosa flower, which matches its sunny color. Britain's Buck's Fizz is a close cousin with more bubbles and less juice.
lookFor: An inexpensive dry sparkling wine (Cava or Prosecco) and pulp-free orange juice.

name: French 75
style: Gin, lemon, sugar, Champagne: crisp, citrusy, elegant
why: Crisp lemon, a little gin and a fizzy Champagne top. Elegant with oysters, seafood and brunch bites.
funFact: It's named after the French 75mm field gun of World War I, because it was said to hit with similar force.
lookFor: Gin, fresh lemon, simple syrup and any dry sparkling wine.

name: Bloody Mary
style: Vodka + spiced tomato juice: savory, tangy, spicy
why: Savory, tangy and a little spicy, almost a meal in a glass. The brunch classic with eggs, bacon and burgers.
funFact: Its origin is disputed, but a popular claim credits bartender Fernand Petiot at Harry's New York Bar in Paris in the 1920s.
factCheck: VERIFY: Fernand Petiot / Harry's New York Bar origin is the most common claim but contested.
lookFor: Vodka, a good Bloody Mary mix, and a celery stalk (plus pickles or olives if you like).

name: Gin Martini
style: Gin + dry vermouth: crisp, herbal, ice-cold
why: Ice-cold, crisp and herbal, a classic grown-up sip. Great with oysters, olives, charcuterie or a steak dinner.
funFact: The original martini was made with gin. Vodka martinis only became popular in the mid-20th century.
lookFor: London Dry gin, dry vermouth and a lemon twist or olive.

name: Whiskey Sour
style: Whiskey, lemon, sugar: tart, sweet, smooth
why: Tart lemon and warm whiskey balanced with a little sugar. Its tang cuts right through burgers, fried chicken and BBQ.
funFact: Sours show up in Jerry Thomas's 1862 bartender's guide, one of the first cocktail books ever published.
lookFor: Bourbon, fresh lemon juice and simple syrup (egg white optional, for foam).

name: Manhattan
style: Whiskey, sweet vermouth, bitters: rich, smooth, spiced
why: Rich, smooth and a little spiced, with a cherry on top. A classic with steak, pork or a charcuterie board.
funFact: A popular story says Winston Churchill's mother invented it at a New York party in the 1870s, but she was in England at the time, so historians consider it a myth.
factCheck: VERIFY: The Jennie Jerome story is widely considered a myth; confirm wording.
lookFor: Rye or bourbon, sweet vermouth, Angostura bitters and a cocktail cherry.

name: Negroni
style: Gin, Campari, sweet vermouth: bittersweet, bold
why: Bittersweet orange and herbs, bold and grown-up. Its bitterness wakes up the palate before pizza, salami and cheese.
funFact: The classic story says Count Camillo Negroni asked a bartender in Florence around 1919 to make his Americano stronger by swapping the soda water for gin.
factCheck: VERIFY: The Count Negroni origin is the standard story but some historians question it.
lookFor: Equal parts gin, Campari and sweet vermouth, with an orange peel.

name: Piña Colada
style: Rum, pineapple, coconut: creamy, sweet, tropical
why: Creamy coconut and sweet pineapple, basically a vacation in a glass. It cools down spicy jerk chicken and loves shrimp and tropical fruit.
funFact: The Piña Colada has been the official national drink of Puerto Rico since 1978.
lookFor: White rum, pineapple juice and cream of coconut, blended with ice.

name: Cosmopolitan
style: Vodka, cranberry, lime, orange liqueur: tart, fruity
why: Tart cranberry and lime with a pretty pink color. A fun, fruity match for appetizers, seafood and cheese.
funFact: The Cosmo was around before, but the TV show Sex and the City made it a worldwide star in the late 1990s.
lookFor: Citrus vodka, triple sec, cranberry juice and fresh lime.

name: Moscow Mule
style: Vodka, ginger beer, lime: spicy-sweet, fizzy
why: Zingy ginger, lime and bubbles over lots of ice. It's refreshing next to tacos, spicy food and burgers.
funFact: It was created in the early 1940s as a way to sell more vodka and ginger beer, and the copper mug became its trademark.
lookFor: Vodka, ginger beer and a lime wedge. A copper mug is fun but optional.

name: Classic Daiquiri
style: Rum, lime, sugar: tart, clean, refreshing
why: Just rum, lime and sugar: bright, tart and refreshing (not the frozen slushie!). Great with ceviche, shrimp and Cuban food.
funFact: It's named after Daiquirí, a beach and small town near Santiago de Cuba.
lookFor: White rum, fresh lime juice and simple syrup, shaken and served straight up.

name: Mai Tai
style: Rum, lime, orange, almond syrup: tropical, rich
why: Tropical, nutty and fruity with a rum kick. Fun with poke, grilled pork and tropical fruit.
funFact: Trader Vic said he created it in Oakland, California in 1944. "Maita'i" is Tahitian for "good."
factCheck: VERIFY: Trader Vic vs. Donn Beach origin is disputed; the 1944 Trader Vic claim is the common version.
lookFor: Aged rum, lime, orange curaçao and orgeat (almond syrup).

name: White Russian
style: Vodka, coffee liqueur, cream: creamy, sweet, dessert-y
why: Coffee, cream and a little vodka, like a boozy iced latte. A cozy dessert match for brownies, chocolate and ice cream.
funFact: It isn't Russian at all; the name comes from the vodka. The Big Lebowski turned it into a cult classic.
lookFor: Vodka, coffee liqueur and heavy cream or whole milk over ice.

name: Lemon Drop
style: Vodka, lemon, sugar rim: sweet-tart, candy-like
why: Sweet-tart lemon with a sugared rim, like grown-up lemonade candy. Bright with seafood, appetizers and cheesecake.
funFact: It's believed to have been invented in San Francisco in the 1970s, named after the classic lemon-drop candy.
factCheck: VERIFY: The 1970s San Francisco (Henry Africa's) origin is commonly cited but not firmly documented.
lookFor: Citrus vodka, fresh lemon, triple sec and simple syrup, with a sugar rim.

name: Dirty Martini
style: Vodka or gin + olive brine: salty, savory, ice-cold
why: Salty, briny and ice-cold, for people who love olives. Great with oysters, fries and a charcuterie board.
funFact: "Dirty" just means a splash of olive brine is added. The more brine, the dirtier it is.
lookFor: Vodka or gin, a little dry vermouth, olive brine and green olives.

name: Mint Julep
style: Bourbon, mint, sugar, crushed ice: cool, sweet, minty
why: Cool mint and sweet bourbon over mounds of crushed ice. A Southern classic with fried chicken, BBQ and pecan pie.
funFact: The Mint Julep has been the official drink of the Kentucky Derby since 1939.
lookFor: Bourbon, fresh mint, simple syrup and lots of crushed ice.

name: Red Sangria
style: Red wine punch with fruit: juicy, sweet, easy
why: Juicy, fruity and made by the pitcher, so everyone is happy. Great with tapas, paella and grilled meats.
funFact: Sangria gets its name from "sangre," Spanish for blood, because of its deep red color. In the EU, only sangria made in Spain or Portugal can be sold under that name.
factCheck: VERIFY: The EU labeling rule (2014 regulation on aromatized wine products) is believed accurate but worth confirming.
lookFor: A cheap Spanish red (like Garnacha), chopped fruit, orange juice and a splash of brandy. Make it ahead.

name: White Sangria
style: White wine punch with peaches and citrus: light, sweet
why: Crisp white wine with peaches, citrus and a little fizz. A lighter, brighter pitcher for seafood, salads, fruit and brunch.
funFact: Red may have given sangria its name, but white versions ("sangría blanca") are popular in Spain too, made with the same fruit-and-wine idea.
lookFor: A dry Spanish white (like Albariño or Verdejo), peaches, citrus and a splash of soda.
